question: Which of the following is a false statement regarding retinitis pigmentosa (RP)?

options.D: bone spicules from RPE dispersion are always present
options.C: central visual acuity can diminish due to macular edema
options.B: the classic visual field on Goldmann testing is a peripheral ring scotoma
options.A: it is predominately a disease of rod dysfunction

explanation: While unusual, RP can occur without bone spicule formation and is termed retinitis pigmentosa sine pigmentum. Bone spicules result from dispersion of pigment in the retinal pigment epithelial layer which leads to the formation of clumps that look similar to bone under the microscope. Usually these cases of RP sine pigmentum have other fundus findings typical of RP including waxy pallor of the optic nerve and attenuated arterioles. Also, bone spicules can occur in many other diseases causing destruction of the retina (e.g., old trauma, diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis, syphilis, etc). • An 8-year-old girl is referred to your clinic for the fundus findings seen above. The fundus photo shows geographic paving-stone-like areas of atrophy that are coalescing to form a scalloped border between abnormal and normal RPE. These fundus abnormalities are typical of gyrate atrophy, an autosomal recessive condition which is caused by a mutation of the OAT gene (chromosome 10). Mutations in this gene result in markedly-high elevations of plasma ornithine which is toxic to the retina and choroid. Treatment consists of dietary arginine restriction (if possible) and vitamin B6 supplementation (if the patient is actually responsive to this therapy). The five most prominent features of this disease include: (1) the gyrate retinal and choroidal lesions; (2) posterior subcapsular cataracts; (3) high myopia with high astigmatism (e.g. -6 to -10 diopters of myopia); (4) autosomal recessive pattern; and (5) hyperornithinemia (if ornithine levels are normal, another diagnosis should be entertained). Visual acuity is usually normal in these patients until the age of 10 years. However, night blindness typically starts in the first decade of life. explanation: This patient has a vitelliform macular lesion with visual symptoms starting in his 40's. The most common cause of this presentation is adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy (AFVD). Mutations in BEST1 are responsible for Best disease and some cases of AFVD. If this were Best disease, his visual symptoms would have started when he was younger. Mutations in PRPH2, IMPG1, and IMPG2 can also be responsible for this dystrophy. However, <25% of individuals with AFVD have mutations in any of the aforementioned genes (i.e. the genetic cause is unknown). Mutations in the ABCA4 gene are responsible for Stargardt's disease with most cases being autosomal recessive in inheritance. This condition is characterized by foveal atrophy surrounded by yellowish, "pisciform flecks" at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium. A fluorescein angiogram may demonstrate the phenomenon of a "dark choroid" which is rather specific to Stargardt disease. Mutations in OAT are responsible for gyrate atrophy. This condition is characterized by geographic paving-stone-like areas of atrophy that coalesce to form a scalloped border between abnormal and normal RPE. Gyrate atrophy is an autosomal recessive condition. Mutations in OAT result in markedly-high elevations of ornithinewhich is toxic to the retina and choroid. Treatment consists of dietary arginine restriction (if possible) and vitamin B6 supplementation (if the patient is actually responsive to this therapy). Other findings in gyrate atrophy include: posterior subcapsular cataracts, and high myopia with high astigmatism. Visual acuity is usually normal in these patients until the age of 10 years. Mutations in TIMP3 gene (on chromosome 22) are responsible for Sorsby macular dystrophy (aka Sorsby pseudoinflammatory fundus dystrophy). The TIMP3 gene encodes for tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-3. This autosomal dominant condition manifests clinically in the affected individual's third to fifth decade of life. Sorsby's may initially present with multiple, fine drusen- like deposits in the paramacular region. These lesions may progress to choroidal neovascularization with subsequent hemorrhagic maculopathy and subretinal fibrosis. explanation: The fundus photo shows a mild, lightly-pigmented fundus. The foveal reflex is also not distinct in this photo. The patient also has cutaneous and hair hypopigmentation; therefore, he has some form of oculocutaneous albinism. Since he apparently has not gained more pigment over the years, he most likely has tyrosinase-negative oculocutaneous albinism. The terms "complete" versus "partial" albinism and "tyrosinase-negative" versus "tyrosinase- positive" albinism have been replaced with a classification scheme based on the specific gene mutation. Regardless, the BCSC still discusses how individuals with tyrosinase-positive oculocutaneous albinism will have slow darkening of their skin, hair, irides, and RPE over time. The BCSC also states that this progressively- increased pigmentation is associated with improved nystagmus and visual acuity over time. This teenager should not be classified as having ocular albinism since he also has skin/hair involvement. Regardless of whether an individual has oculocutaneous albinism or ocular albinism, his/her ocular involvement may follow one of two clinical patterns: true albinism or albinoidism. "Albinoidism" is a generic term used to describe a milder clinical pattern of ocular involvement. "Albinoidism" confers milder visual consequences with normal development of the fovea while "true albinism" implies poor vision with a hypoplastic fovea (e.g. loss of foveal pit/reflex and non evident luteal pigment). The gold standard for diagnosing true albinism is flash and pattern VEPs (visual evoked potentials). Both of these ocular clinical pattners share the features of photophobia, iris transillumination defects, and hypopigmented fundi. Interestingly, the temporal nerve fibers decussate instead of projecting to the ipsilateral lateral geniculate body in all forms of albinism. As discussed in a separate question in this section, one should inquire about other systemic symptoms when a patient is diagnosed with albinism. Such systemic symptoms may be the harbinger of serious diseases associated with albinism like Chédiak-Higashi syndrome or Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome. A brief summary of these potentially life-threatening diseases: • Chédiak-Higashi syndrome o albinism + neutropenia o extreme susceptibility to infections o bleeding problems (mildly deficient platelets) o neurological symptoms in early adulthood (e.g. ataxia, peripheral neuropathy) • Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome o albinism + platelet defect (easy bleeding/bruising) o associated with Puerto Rican descent in the United States o sometimes associated with pulmonary fibrosis, granulomatous colitis, and immunodeficiency • • A 42-year-old man presents to your clinic with symptoms of slowly declining central visual acuity over the past few years. explanation: The fundus photo shows well-defined and bilaterally symmetric central areas of atrophy which affect the RPE and choriocapillaris. As a result, the large choroidal vessels are readily seen underneath. In older patients, this appearance could simulate the geographic atrophy that occurs in some age-related degeneration patients. However, given the apparent autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, age of onset in middle age, lack of abnormalities on electrophysiologic studies, and relatively normal choroidal flush, this patient most likely has central areolar choroidal dystrophy (CACD). CACD is caused by mutations in the peripherin/RDS gene (PRPH2) and is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern (although some autosomal recessive cases have been reported). The age of onset is in the 30-60 years of age and the presenting visual acuity is typically in the 20/25 to 20/200 range. Early fundus findings include a mild degree of nonspecific granularity of the fovea which slowly progresses to the pathognomonic round zone of neurosensory, RPE, and choriocapillary atrophy seen above. Unlike Best's disease, where the EOG is always abnormal, electrophysiologic studies are normal in CACD except in advanced cases. Unlike Stargardt's disease which presents with a diffusely-"silent choroid" on FA, the choroidal flush is mostly normal in CACD. Also, inheritance in Stargardt's is usually in an autosomal recessive pattern. Patients with North Carolina macular dystrophy typically reach their final visual acuity (~20/50-20/200) by late puberty, which contrasts the later onset of CACD. explanation: The vignette is alluding to the condition known as fundus albipunctatus (FA). This is a rare, hereditary, and typically stationary retinal disease. It is characterized by the following attributes: • Many small white/yellow lesions distributed throughout the retina except the fovea. • Normal optic discs and retinal vessels (unlike retinitis pigmentosa). • Visual acuity, visual fields, and color vision are typically normal (unless a dim stimulus is used). A dim environment will cause worsening of visual acuity and a constriction of the visual field. • Rod electroretinogram (ERG) is minimal but normalizes after the patient spends several hours in a dark environment. • Non-progressive. FA is typically inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. The vast majority of cases are caused by mutations in the RDH5 gene which encodes 11-cis retinol dehydrogenase, which is located in the retinal pigment epithelium and is involved in the visual cycle (i.e. regeneration of the visual pigment, rhodopsin). The main differential diagnosis of FA is retinitis punctata albescens (RPA). Though they have similar (confusing) names, they are completely different entities. Though both conditions can feature yellow/white dots, retinitis punctata albescens is a varient of retinitis pigmentosa and thus also features narrowed retinal vessels, optic disc pallor, and a severely-depressed ERG that does not recover with dark adaptation. Visual acuity and fields are progressively affected with RPA and the fundus in older individuals can have other hallmarks of retinitis pigmentosa like bone spicules. RPA is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and is caused by mutations in the RLBP1 gene (retinaldehyde binding protein 1) which is also involved in the visual cycle. Mutations in this gene can also rarely cause some forms of FA. Mutations in the ABCA4 gene are responsible for most cases of Stargardt disease. Other diseases associated with mutations in this gene include cone-rod dystrophy, retinitis pigmentosa, and fundus flavimaculatus (variant of Stargardt). Mutations in the RDS/peripherin gene are typically associated with the pattern dystrophies (e.g. adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy, butterfly dystrophy). However, mutations in this gene can also cause Stargardt disease. • Q-You are examining a 10-month-old child as a consult on the pediatric ward. explanation: The photo on the left shows macular pigment mottling while the photo on the right shows polydactyly. This teenager is also obese and his vision difficulties began with night vision. These findings and history are most consistent with a diagnosis of Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS). Individuals with BBS may also have a pigmentary retinopathy that resembles retinitis pigmentosa (RP), albeit usually without classic bone-spicules. They typically begin with night vision problems, then peripheral vision problems, and finally also with central vision loss by early adulthood. Other key features of BBS are intellectual disability, hypogonadism, and renal failure There is some overlap between BBS and Laurence-Moon syndrome (LMS) and some authors consider them to be on the continuum of the same syndrome. Classically however, LMS features spastic paraplegia and does NOT have polydactyly. Alström syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder chararacterized by a tapetoretinal degeneration, obesity, diabetes, hearing loss, renal failure, and dilated cardiomyopathy. Unlike the other pigmentary retinopathies, central vision is lost early in Alström syndrome. Unlike BBS, there is no polydactyly, hypogonadism, or intellectual disability in these patients. explanation: Stargardt disease, or fundus flavimaculatus, is an inherited juvenile cone-rod dystrophy that causes progressive vision loss with final visual acuity ranging from 20/50-20/200. The progression usually starts between the ages of six and twelve years old; the rate of progression is quite variable. The characteristic fundus appearance in Stargardt disease includes yellow parafoveal “pisciform” flecks with peripapillary sparing and a “beaten bronze” macula. Present in about 80% of cases and a very specific finding, a dark choroid is believed to be a blocking phenomena whereby lipofuscin-like material accumulates in the retinal pigment epithelial layer and prevents transmission of fluorescence from the choroid below. Fluorescein quenching is an idiopathic rapid clearing of fluorescein in patients with Birdshot chorioretinopathy. Expansile dot leakage from the choriocapillaris into the subretinal space occurs in central serous chorioretinopathy (along with the “chimney stack” leakage pattern). Patchy, delayed choroidal filling is typical of choroidal ischemia in giant cell arteritis although can occur in other choroidopathies such as hypertensive choroidopathy or Wegener granulomatosis-associated choroidopathy. • Q-A 25-year-old patient with a history of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa presents with decreased central vision OS over the last month. explanation: Choroideremia is an X-linked recessive disease which is caused by mutations of the CHM gene. This gene encodes for a geranylgeranyl transferase Rab escort protein. The general progression of fundus changes is: • Starts as mottled areas of pigmentation in the anterior equatorial region and macula. • These affected anterior areas degenerate to confluent scalloped areas of RPE and choriocapillaris loss. • There is typically no change in the retinal vasculature or optic atrophy. The differential diagnosis of choroideremia is gyrate atrophy, Bietti crystalline dystrophy, and thioridazine retinal toxicity. Histologic studies have localized the CHM gene product to the RPE. Therefore, the basic defect in this disease involves the RPE (not the choriocapillaris). Most patients with this disease maintain good visual acuity for 4 or 5 decades. There is no known treatment for choroideremia though gene therapy holds some future promise. Carriers of the CHM mutation are typically asymptomatic and have normal ERG results. However, carriers often show patches of subretinal black mottled pigment or a lobular pattern of RPE and choriocapillaris loss. explanation: Perfluorocarbon liquid (PFCL) is most commonly employed during repair of complex retinal detachments such as those due to giant retinal tears or complicated by proliferative vitreoretinopathy. Properties of PFCL that contribute to its usefulness include: • High specific gravity relative to saline, resulting in excellent retinal tamponade • Low viscosity, allowing easy injection and removal • High boiling point, avoiding vaporization with endophotocoagulation during surgery • High surface tension, allowing the liquid to remain as a single bubble Subfoveal retained perfluorocarbon liquid (PFCL) is a rare but serious complication associated with retinal detachment repair. Optical coherence tomography reveals characteristic large hyporeflective spaces corresponding to retained PFCL bubbles. PFCL is toxic when in direct contact with the retina for prolonged periods and subfoveal PFCL may result in permanent vision loss. explanation: A small TRD that does not threaten the macula does not require vitrectomy. These TRDs may remain stable for a prolonged length of time and may be managed with careful follow-up with possible panretinal photocoagulation if there are high-risk characteristics present. If a TRD threatens or involves the macula, then immediate vitrectomy is generally recommended. Scleral buckle and pneumatic retinopexy are modalities usually reserved for repair of rhegmetogenous retinal detachments. explanation: The two strongest risk factors for the development of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) are gestational age (GA) and birth weight (BW). The importance of these two risk factors is reflected in the American Academy of Ophthalmology and American Academy of Pediatrics' guidelines which state that all infants ≤30 weeks of GA or ≤1,500 grams of BW should be screened for ROP. Another major risk factor for the development of severe ROP is the use of supplemental oxygen. However, though decreased supplemental oxygen use decreases the incidence of ROP, it also results in higher infant morbidity and mortality. Beyond those three major risk factors, many other factors increase the incidence of ROP: • Respiratory distress disorder (RDS). This condition is caused by a surfactant deficiency in the neonate. The increased incidence of ROP in neonates with RDS is logical since these infants require mechanical ventilation and supplemental oxygen use. • Transfusion of red blood cells. Many studies support that the need for blood transfusions is a risk factor for ROP. However, there is conflicting evidence whether anemia itself is an independent risk factor. • Thrombocytopenia. • Neonatal sepsis. • Low postnatal weight gain. Slow weight gain is also associated with a lower postnatal increase of serum insulin growth factor-1 (IGF-1). IGF-1 is a hormone that promotes the development of several tissues including retinal vessels. There is conflicting evidence whether or not male gender increases the rate of ROP. Caffeine is commonly administered for the treatment and prophylaxis of apnea of prematurity. There are several studies that have found that severe ROP was less common in infants assigned to caffeine. question: If OCT imaging were to be obtained through the finding, which of the following layers would be abnormal?
explanation: The finding in the photo is commotio retinae. In the setting of blunt trauma to the front of the eye, the retina can develop a gray-white discoloration due to damage to the outer retinal layers, specifically the photoreceptors and RPE. Affected areas may be confined to the posterior pole causing decreased vision or involve extensive areas of peripheral retina with no visual symptoms. The outer retinal whitening will resolve over weeks and may leave no abnormal fundus findings, or may cause mottling of the RPE, pigment migration, or rarely full-thickness macular hole formation if in the posterior pole. Recovery of the affected cells range from complete recovery to contusion necrosis causing outer retinal atrophy and loss of the RPE. Fluorescein angiography initially reveals no alterations in retinal or choroidal perfusion in the area of commotio but may show staining of the RPE. Later, window defects may be present due to RPE atrophy. Acutely, OCT shows increased reflectivity and disruption of the photoreceptor layers followed by either loss of the photoreceptors and RPE or complete normalization of the OCT depending on the extent of the injury. Originally, commotio retinae was thought to be caused by retinal edema (i.e. extracellular accumulation of fluid). Thus, the previous term of "Berlin edema." However, this cause of retinal whitening now has been found to be caused by disruption in the architecuture of the photoreceptor elements. Commotio retinae is most commonly found in the macula, but can occur anywhere in the retina. When it involves the macula, it can appear as a "cherry red spot" since the cells involved in the whitening are not present in the fovea. "Amyloidosis" is a generic term that is used to describe the deposition of fibrils which are composed of low molecular weight (5 to 25 kD) subunits of a variety of proteins. Many of these proteins are normal substances found in the serum. These fibrils undergo an abnormal conformational change into the classic antiparallel beta-pleated sheet. These abnormal proteins deposit into various organs within the body causing their dysfunction. All these protein aggregates classically stain with Congo Red and show apple-green birefringence with dichroism under polarized light. There are at least 30 different human protein precursors which can result in "amyloidosis." A full discussion of all the various forms of amyloidosis are well beyond the scope of this website. However, there are only a few forms of amyloidosis that you really need to remember since they involve the eye: Mutations in the transthyretin (TTR) gene • The TTR gene is located on chromosome 18. Transthyretin was previously known as prealbumin. • Though >120 TTR mutations have been described, the most common ones cause something called "familial amyloid polyneuropathy (FAP) types I and II". • Systemic manifestations include upper/lower extremity polyneuropathy, central nervous system abnormalities, cardiomyopathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, and gastrointestinal/renal abnormalities. • Classic ocular manifestation: bilateral vitreous opacification associated with retinal hemorrhages/exudates/cotton-wool spots, and peripheral retinal neovascularization. Dr. Stanley Chang's seminal work (published in the American Journal of Ophthalmology) on this subject found the following: • Among pre-op glaucoma suspects, the mean IOP was 19.5 ± 2.7 mm Hg in the vitrectomized eye, compared with 14.3 ± 3.0 mm Hg in the fellow eye (p = .0001). • Among eyes where glaucoma only developed after vitrectomy, the time interval between vitrectomy and the diagnosis of glaucoma was significantly longer (45.95 ± 44.79 months) in phakic eyes compared to nonphakic eyes (18.39 ± 13.76 months) (p = .0115). In other words, presence of the lens appeared protective against glaucoma. • Among eyes already being treated for glaucoma pre-op, the mean number of glaucoma medications was higher (2.9 ± 1.2) in the vitrectomized eye compared to the fellow (non-vitrectomized) eye (2.00 ± 1.4; p = .0215). explanation: Terson syndrome is characterized by vitreous and sub-internal limiting membrane or sub-hyaloid hemorrhage caused by an acute intracranial hemorrhage. The proposed mechanism for these multi-level hemorrhages is that the acute intracranial hemorrhage causes an acute rise in intraocular venous pressure. It is estimated that 1/3 of patients with subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhage have Terson syndrome. Typically, the hemorrhage associated with Terson syndrome clears spontaneously and visual function is not severely affected once the blood clears. The main condition that is differentiated from Terson syndrome after acute trauma is Purtscher retinopathy. In this latter condition, the fundus appearance is characterized by large cotton-wool spots, hemorrhages, and retinal edema most commonly surrounding the optic disc (see image below). Optic atrophy (and thus permanent vision loss) is more common in Purtscher retinopathy compared to Terson syndrome and is thought to be caused by injury-induced complement activation which results in granulocyte aggregation and leukoembolization. This cascade then occludes small arterioles, especially of the peripapillary retina. Other conditions that do not involve trauma can exhibit findings similar to Purtscher retinopathy. In these non-traumatic cases, the fundus findings are called "Purtscher- like" retinopathy. Causes of Purtscher-like retinopathy include: acute pancreatitis, collagen-vascular diseases, childbirth, and amniotic fluid embolism. explanation: The fundus and red-free photos depict a bullous, "dome-shaped" elevation of the retina. These photos, along with the absence of vitreous hemorrhage/pigment, inferotemporal location, and absence of shifting fluid, are characteristics of degenerative retinoschisis. Retinoschisis is a splitting of the neurosensory retina which can resemble a retinal detachment. Other features that differentiate retinoschisis from a retinal detachment include: absolute scotoma, positive reaction to photocoagulation, and absence of corrugation. Degenerative retinoschisis is sometimes subdivided into typical and reticular forms. In typical degenerative retinoschisis, the splitting occurs in the outer plexiform layer while in reticular degenerative retinoschisis, the splitting occurs in the nerve fiber layer. Posterior extension of the schisis cavity is more common in the reticular form Retinal detachment can occur with retinoschisis, but it is a relatively rare occurrence. For example, previous studies have found retinoschisis to be present in 6% of rhegmatogenous retinal detachments (RRDs), but retinoschisis was only responsible for less than 2.5% of RRDs. In general, there are two patterns of retinal detachment that can occur with retinoschisis. The first pattern is a localized and stable form with outer retinal holes only. The second pattern is a symptomatic and rapidly-progressive detachment with both inner and outer layer holes. Only treatment for the latter type of retinal detachment is necessary. Prophylactic treatment is NOT recommended for asymptomatic patients with retinoschisis or with localized retinal detachments since complications can occur (e.g. new retinal breaks, vitreous hemorrhage). explanation: Of the peripheral retinal lesions listed, only meridional folds (MFs) are associated with an increased risk of retinal detachment. MFs are folds of redundant peripheral retina that project into the vitreous. They are either aligned with a dentate process or with the middle of an ora bay. MFs are most commonly found in the superonasal quadrant. They are present in approximately 20% of all eyes. A meridional complex is when a dentate process and ciliary process occur within the same meridian. The involved dentate and ciliary processes are typically abnormally large, combined with a meridional fold, and usually associated with peripheral retinal excavation along the same meridian. Cobblestone degeneration describes small, discrete areas of atrophy of the outer retina. It is most common in the inferior quadrants and is present in approximately one-fifth of all people. The presence of cobblestone actually prevents the spread of a retinal detachment. Peripheral cystoid degeneration describes zones of microcysts in the far peripheral retina.
